content.headline: Deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh airport raises risk of wider war
content.shortHeadline: Riyadh airport attack raises risk of wider war
content.standfirst: Saudi Arabia has blamed the Iran-backed Houthis for a missile strike that killed 12 people and injured more than 300. The coalition in Yemen has vowed to respond as Washington weighs its next move.

image.caption: Dust and debris inside King Khalid International Airport after Saturday’s attack.

sources.originalTitle: Saudi coalition vows retaliation after deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh airport
Riyadh airport attack another dangerous moment in already tense conflict

segments.body: A suspected Houthi missile attack damaged King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday, killing 12 people and wounding more than 300, according to The Guardian. Saudi authorities extended the airport closure and moved schools online until Thursday. The Saudi-led coalition said it would “respond firmly”; the Houthis warned airlines, passengers and staff to stay away from Saudi airports.

segments.title: Regional stakes
segments.body: The attack comes amid renewed fighting in Yemen and a wider regional conflict involving Iran, the United States and Israel. The Guardian reports that the US has so far provided intelligence and targeting support, but not directly joined the campaign against the Houthis. It warns that direct US involvement could put Red Sea shipping at greater risk.

perspectives.body: BBC analysis focuses on the Houthis’ ability to strike strategic infrastructure and shipping routes, arguing that Saudi Arabia’s reputation for stability is also at stake. It says President Trump signalled he might intervene, but that another US conflict could carry domestic political costs.

content.headline: Trump calls for new Ukrainian leader after diesel deal with Russia
content.shortHeadline: Trump urges Ukraine to replace Zelensky after diesel deal
content.standfirst: The US president’s agreement to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports has deepened a dispute with Kyiv. Trump criticised Volodymyr Zelensky, while Ukraine says it would halt strikes on Russian energy sites if Moscow does the same.

image.caption: Rescuers evacuate a wounded woman from a building hit by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia.

sources.originalTitle: 'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel deal
Trump says Ukraine needs a new leader after diesel deal with Russia
Trump’s Putin deal is a desperate attempt to win voters – Ukraine will pay for it
Trump says Ukraine and Russia have agreed 'energy ceasefire'
Britain stands behind Zelenskyy, says Streeting after Trump’s call for new leader in Ukraine
Analytiker efter ny omgang skældud til Zelenskyj: 'Trump er sprunget ud af skabet'

segments.body: Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to get a new president after Volodymyr Zelensky criticised a US-Russia agreement to release Russian diesel for sale. Trump said the deal would help supply markets and blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries for worsening fuel pressures. Ukraine says the strikes target revenue and infrastructure supporting Russia’s war.

segments.title: A disputed route to a truce
segments.body: Zelensky said Russian energy revenues would help fund the invasion and pointed to deadly Russian strikes on Zaporizhzhia after the deal was announced. He has said Ukraine is willing to stop attacks on Russian energy infrastructure if Russia stops targeting Ukraine’s. Trump later said the two sides had agreed to an immediate “energy ceasefire”; neither Kyiv nor Moscow had confirmed that assertion in the BBC’s report.

content.headline: Myanmar junta’s conscription drive fuels fear of abductions and forced service
content.shortHeadline: Myanmar’s conscription drive fuels fear of forced recruitment
content.standfirst: Young men in one town say they fear being seized and sent to fight as the military struggles to fill its ranks. BBC reporting describes alleged coercion, extortion and the sale of recruits by local officials.

image.caption: Authorities in Myanmar have been ordered to meet military recruitment quotas, according to BBC reporting.

sources.originalTitle: Young men live in fear of being snatched off the streets and sold to Myanmar's army

segments.body: Young men in Hpa-An, in Myanmar’s Karen state, say they are staying home after dark and limiting where they travel amid reports of people being taken for military service. BBC Burmese reports that leaked documents show officials were ordered to meet recruitment quotas as the junta faces resistance from ethnic militias and pro-democracy groups. The authorities declined to comment on allegations of forced recruitment and abductions.

segments.title: A recruitment system under pressure
segments.body: The BBC reports that Myanmar’s conscription law requires men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve, and that an estimated 100,000 young people have been recruited in the past two and a half years. Rights groups say recruitment has involved coercion and abduction. One woman told the BBC that local officials allegedly transferred her husband to another ward to meet its quota; an administrator acknowledged arranging the transfer but denied money was involved.

content.headline: At least 109 migrants dead after boat capsizes off Djibouti
content.shortHeadline: At least 109 dead after migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti
content.standfirst: The boat was carrying about 350 people from Djibouti towards Yemen when it capsized near Obock. The UN migration agency says about 80 people were rescued and dozens remain missing.

image.caption: A migrant boat pictured in April 2026 on the route between Djibouti and Yemen.

sources.originalTitle: Children among 109 dead after boat capsizes off Djibouti, UN says

segments.body: At least 109 people, including 15 children, died when a boat capsized off Djibouti on Thursday night, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said. It was carrying about 350 people and capsized near the port town of Obock while travelling towards Yemen. About 80 people were rescued, and dozens more are still missing.

segments.title: A dangerous, continuing route
segments.body: The IOM says tens of thousands of people from the Horn of Africa make the journey each year, hoping to reach Gulf countries. More than 900 migrants died or went missing on the route in 2025, while the agency recorded more than 20,000 movements from Ethiopia to Djibouti from 10 September. Survivors are receiving medical care and help to reconnect with family.

content.headline: Drone strike kills 41 people at displaced people’s gathering in Sudan
content.shortHeadline: Rights group says Sudan drone strike killed 41
content.standfirst: The Rapid Support Forces are accused of attacking a gathering of displaced people in Blue Nile state. The UN says initial reports indicate that most of the casualties were women and children.

sources.originalTitle: Drone strike by Sudan paramilitary kills 41 near Ethiopian border, rights group says

segments.body: A drone strike killed 41 people in Sudan’s Blue Nile region, including eight children, the rights group Emergency Lawyers said. The group said the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) targeted a gathering of displaced people in Abu Shandi on Friday. The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said initial reports suggested most casualties were women and children.

Sudan’s army and the RSF have been fighting for power since 2023. The war has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced more than 14 million people, according to the BBC report. Both sides have been accused of drone attacks; the UN says the area reportedly struck had been under sustained attack in recent weeks.

content.headline: Polish schools on alert after attacks leave one dead and others hurt
content.shortHeadline: Poland investigates school attacks after fatal stabbing
content.standfirst: Three attacks at educational institutions left a caretaker dead and others injured, according to the Polish prime minister. Police say they have detained people over weapons and threats as schools respond to rumours of further violence.

image.caption: A caretaker was killed at a primary school north of Warsaw this week.

sources.originalTitle: Poland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk says
Frygt for "blodig fredag" spreder sig i Polen – lørdag blev endnu en skole ramt
Polsk politi har modtaget oplysninger om planlagt angreb mod Polens premierminister

segments.body: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three attacks at schools this week were driven by the “glorification of violence” online. One attack killed a caretaker and others injured pupils and staff. Police have searched schools and detained people over possession of weapons or threats to attack schools, though published reports give different totals.

segments.title: Threats and unanswered questions
segments.body: Tusk said the attacks were not part of a large organised group, while describing some detainees as active in far-right circles. Separately, Polish security services met after receiving information about a possible attack on Tusk and Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. Authorities said they were treating the threat seriously; the available reports do not establish a connection between it and the school attacks.

content.headline: Polish police arrest man suspected of planning attack on Donald Tusk
content.shortHeadline: Man arrested over suspected plot against Poland’s Tusk
content.standfirst: Poland’s interior minister says police arrested a man suspected of threatening and planning an attack on the prime minister. Authorities have released few details about the alleged plot or its timing.

image.caption: Polish officials have released no further details about the suspected attack plot.

sources.originalTitle: Polsk politi har anholdt mand efter trusler mod Donald Tusk
Polsk politi har modtaget oplysninger om planlagt angreb mod Polens premierminister

segments.body: Polish police have arrested a man suspected of threatening and planning an attack on Prime Minister Donald Tusk, Interior Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said. Officials had earlier described information about a possible attack on Tusk and Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz as especially concerning and said they were taking it seriously.

Authorities have not disclosed where or when the alleged attack was intended to happen, or who may have been involved beyond the arrested man. The arrest followed a meeting of security officials. A separate report says authorities assessed that there was a high likelihood the threat could be carried out, but provides no further information about its basis.

content.headline: US investigates five TV networks after White House pool coverage boycott
content.shortHeadline: US probes TV networks over White House coverage boycott
content.standfirst: The Justice Department is examining whether five broadcasters broke competition law when they paused shared coverage after reporters lost White House access. A judge later restored access to the excluded outlets.

image.caption: The dispute over White House press access disrupted shared television coverage of President Trump.

sources.originalTitle: US justice department investigates TV networks over Trump pool coverage
Amerikansk ministerium efterforsker tv-stationer efter boykot af Trump

segments.body: The US Justice Department has asked ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News for communications about their decision to pause presidential pool coverage for several days. The department says it is investigating whether the broadcasters violated federal competition law. The networks have not commented.

segments.title: Press access dispute
segments.body: The boycott followed the White House’s withdrawal of credentials from reporters at CNN, MS Now and Politico. Those outlets sued, arguing that the restrictions violated press freedom, and a judge ordered their access restored. The administration had also changed control of the press pool and restricted Associated Press journalists’ access; the AP’s case remains ongoing, the BBC reports.

content.headline: MPs seek to restore routes for victims to sue police over serious failings
content.shortHeadline: MPs challenge police immunity ruling over serious failings
content.standfirst: A cross-party amendment would narrow a Court of Appeal ruling that blocks many civil claims over police investigations. Its supporters say victims need a route to challenge grave misconduct; the government says the issue should be considered alongside a wider review.

sources.originalTitle: MPs seek to overturn ruling that stops police being sued for failings

segments.body: MPs Andrew Mitchell and Jess Phillips are seeking to change the law after a 2025 Court of Appeal judgment extended police immunity from civil claims relating to criminal investigations. Their amendment would remove that protection in specified cases of serious failure, including alleged fabrication of evidence, dishonesty or negligence.

segments.title: A case at the centre of the dispute
segments.body: The case involved a domestic abuse survivor whose refuge address was included in a file sent to prosecutors and later disclosed in court, forcing her to flee again. The Centre for Women’s Justice warns the ruling could create an “accountability gap”. The government says changes should be considered alongside its review of police accountability; a separate Supreme Court appeal is also due.

content.headline: Farmers warn rising costs and climate shocks threaten UK food security
content.shortHeadline: Farmers warn mounting pressures threaten UK food supply
content.standfirst: Higher fuel and fertiliser costs follow the UK’s record-hot summer and poor cereals harvest. An inquiry by MPs will examine whether the country is prepared for overlapping shocks to its food supply.

image.caption: NFU crops board chair Jamie Burrows says farmers face multiple pressures.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Some aren’t going to make it’: how pressure on farmers threatens UK food security

segments.body: Farmers are preparing fields for the next crop as the price of red diesel has almost doubled since the Iran conflict began, while fertiliser and animal-feed costs have risen by about a fifth, the Guardian reports. The UK also recorded its hottest summer and worst cereals harvest, increasing pressure on producers already dealing with higher operating costs.

segments.title: Planning for disruption
segments.body: The UK produces about 60% of the food it needs and relies on a concentrated distribution network and a small number of ports for imports, according to the reporting. MPs are due to begin hearings on supply-chain resilience after concerns that previous emergency planning did not adequately include food businesses. Experts point to climate and geopolitical shocks among the risks.

content.headline: Review warns ADHD and autism diagnoses are nearing prevalence estimates
content.shortHeadline: Report warns of possible overdiagnosis of ADHD and autism
content.standfirst: A government-commissioned review says diagnoses among some young people are approaching or exceeding estimated prevalence, but stresses that the figures alone do not prove widespread overdiagnosis. It also describes long waits for assessment.

image.caption: The review examines rising diagnoses of ADHD and autism.

sources.originalTitle: The four reasons why ADHD experts fear the UK is heading towards overdiagnosis

segments.body: A review commissioned by the Department of Health and Social Care says NHS diagnosis rates for ADHD and autism among children and young people are rising towards, and in some groups beyond, estimates of how common the conditions are. It says this does not by itself establish that overdiagnosis is occurring at scale, but warns the balance between underdiagnosis and overdiagnosis may be changing.

segments.title: No simple test
segments.body: The report points to broader definitions, greater awareness and subjective assessments among possible reasons for rising diagnoses. It also raises concerns about incentives and the regulation of private assessment clinics. Experts quoted in the report stress that a warning about risk is not proof of a diagnosis being wrong, and that overdiagnosis can coexist with people who still cannot access needed assessment and support.

content.headline: Flu activity in England rose earlier than usual, experts say
content.shortHeadline: Experts urge eligible groups to get flu vaccine early
content.standfirst: Flu indicators were higher in September than during the same period in the previous four winters, though activity remains low. Experts say an early rise does not necessarily mean a more severe season.

image.caption: Flu vaccination is available free on the NHS to eligible groups and privately at pharmacies.

sources.originalTitle: Flu cases higher than usual in England during September, experts say

segments.body: The UK Health Security Agency says flu trends have been rising since August and activity in September was higher than in the same month of each of the past four winters. Emergency-department attendances for influenza-like illness were also above seasonal expectations, although overall flu levels remain low.

segments.title: Vaccination and uncertainty
segments.body: Experts urge people eligible for a free NHS flu vaccine, especially those at higher risk, to get vaccinated before cases peak; it takes weeks for protection to build. An earlier season may mean a longer period of transmission, but experts say timing alone cannot predict severity. The vaccine covers the flu subtypes currently reported in England, though the effect of a small change to one strain is not yet clear.

content.headline: Small-boat crossings continue after UK-France return scheme ends
content.shortHeadline: Crossings persist after UK-France returns pilot ends
content.standfirst: The “one in, one out” scheme moved about 1,500 people in each direction before ending. Refugees and aid groups say people will keep risking the Channel crossing without safer legal routes; others argue cooperation on returns should continue.

image.caption: People flee tear gas as police intervene during an attempted Channel crossing near Calais.

sources.originalTitle: People smugglers are still profiting from small boats. Can the UK fix the crisis?

segments.body: The UK’s “one in, one out” pilot with France has ended after moving approximately 1,500 people in each direction. The Guardian reports that asylum seekers were still gathering in northern France and seeking to cross the Channel. Between 2 and 7 October, 1,739 people arrived in 23 boats, according to figures cited in the report.

segments.title: Routes, returns and risks
segments.body: Aid groups argue that safe, legal routes would reduce reliance on smugglers and the danger of crossings; a union and refugee charity propose a visa-to-travel scheme for people to make asylum claims in the UK. A policy analyst who supported the pilot instead argues that a new “routes for returns” agreement with European partners could build on cooperation. The pilot’s limited scale leaves its effect on crossings uncertain.

content.headline: Right to Buy backlog threatens councils’ plans to build social housing
content.shortHeadline: Right to Buy backlog threatens council housebuilding plans
content.standfirst: Councils expect thousands of delayed home sales to continue, despite forecasts that the 2024 surge would fade. Local authorities and housing experts say replacements may lag behind sales, while ministers argue their reforms will increase social housing over time.

image.caption: The analysis finds expected Right to Buy sales exceed the government’s forecast for replacement homes.

sources.originalTitle: Council housebuilding plan thrown into disarray by Right to Buy surge

segments.body: A backlog of applications to buy council homes is expected to keep Right to Buy sales high into the next two years, undermining government assumptions that sales would quickly fall after discounts were reduced in 2024. The i Paper’s analysis of council information found more than 14,000 homes are expected to be sold this year and next, against 10,450 replacements forecast by the government.

segments.title: A contested route to replacement homes
segments.body: Councils say delays in processing applications are extending the pressure on housing stock, and some want further restrictions on sales. Housing experts warn that sale receipts are often insufficient to fund replacements. The housing ministry says its reforms and planned investment will mean more social homes are built than sold over the next decade.

content.headline: Polanski calls for Green Party structures to change after divisive vote
content.shortHeadline: Polanski signals Green Party reform after Zionism row
content.standfirst: The Green leader says rapid membership growth calls for stronger leadership over strategy, after a disputed conference motion exposed divisions over party democracy and Israel-Palestine policy.

image.caption: Green Party leader Zack Polanski at the party’s autumn conference.

sources.originalTitle: Zack Polanski signals Green party overhaul after row over Zionism vote

segments.body: Zack Polanski has called for changes to the Green Party’s decision-making structures, saying leaders should have more responsibility for setting strategic direction as membership grows. His intervention follows a conference vote declaring Zionism a form of racism, which passed by 1,022 votes to 813 and drew criticism from within the party and the European Green Party.

segments.title: Disagreement over policy and process
segments.body: Polanski says the party should not dictate what members believe and objects to parts of the motion, including its prescription for the future shape of Israel and Palestine. He also says the motion’s substance reflects his understanding of Zionism. Critics argue the vote shows that a small proportion of members can determine policy; supporters of the current system and party figures disagree over what reform should look like.

content.headline: Plan 2 graduates describe debts rising despite monthly repayments
content.shortHeadline: Plan 2 graduates face debts that keep growing
content.standfirst: Three university friends ended up with sharply different student-loan balances as their earnings and circumstances diverged. Their experiences bring renewed scrutiny of Plan 2 terms ahead of the government’s Budget.

image.caption: Lizzy, Charlotte and Libby studied at Newcastle in the year Plan 2 loans were introduced in England.

sources.originalTitle: Three friends on their student debt: One paid off, one chipping away and one creeping up

segments.body: Three friends who began university in England in 2012 each borrowed about £37,500, but their loans have developed very differently. One has cleared her balance with help from family; another says her debt has stayed near £47,000 despite earning £72,000; a third says interest has outpaced repayments on a salary of about £50,000.

segments.title: Who benefits from paying early?
segments.body: Plan 2 loans are written off after 30 years. The BBC reports that finance experts caution that voluntary repayments may only benefit people confident they will repay the loan in full; smaller overpayments can mean paying money unnecessarily. Graduates and campaigners want changes to interest and repayment thresholds, while the Department for Education says it is working to make the system fairer and financially sustainable.

content.headline: Data breach exposes nearly 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers, DR reports
content.shortHeadline: Nearly 8.8 million CPR numbers exposed in data breach
content.standfirst: DR reports that a Danish software company’s compromised access to the CPR register is at the centre of the country’s largest leak of personal identity numbers and addresses. No suspect has been charged.

image.caption: DR reports that a password used by the company appeared in an earlier data leak.

sources.originalTitle: Afsløring: Fynsk virksomhed er centrum for massivt CPR-databrud

segments.body: A small software company on Funen with legal access to the CPR register is at the centre of a major leak of Danish identity numbers and addresses, DR reports. Politiken has seen documentation concerning nearly 8.8 million CPR numbers taken from the system. DR says it has not been able to reach the company, and has not named it while seeking comment.

segments.title: How the breach was detected
segments.body: The CPR administration blocked the company’s access after an unusually high bill triggered an alert, according to documents obtained by DR. The data theft reportedly occurred between 10 and 20 September. DR found that a password used by the company had appeared in an earlier data leak, but says it cannot confirm whether that access was used in this incident. Investigators have not announced any suspects.

content.headline: TV 2 finds passenger planes were overhead during shots at suspected drones
content.shortHeadline: Passenger planes were overhead during shots at suspected drones
content.standfirst: Flight data show aircraft were in the area on two nights when soldiers fired at suspected drones in 2025. Former fighter pilots say lights from planes could have been mistaken for drones; the military maintains its targets were drones.

image.caption: Army commander Peter Boysen presents information about the 2025 incident that TV 2 compared with flight data.

source.credit: Foto: Martin Sylvest / Ritzau Scanpix / TV 2

sources.originalTitle: Data afslører nyt sammenfald: To gange var passagerfly i luften under skud mod droner

segments.body: TV 2’s review of flight data and military information found passenger aircraft in the sky during both incidents when soldiers fired at suspected drones near Borris training camp in September 2025. The newly reported incident was on 25 September. The military says soldiers fired at drones and that an aircraft at about 11.8 kilometres altitude was not relevant to its review.

segments.title: What can be judged in darkness?
segments.body: Two former fighter pilots told TV 2 they could not rule out confusion between aircraft lights and drones, saying distance is difficult to judge at night and modern aircraft lights can appear particularly bright. TV 2 says an aircraft’s route crossed an area shown on the military’s map, but it has not been given the precise time shots were fired. The military stands by its account.

content.headline: DR finds seven Eastern European workers killed in Denmark since 2023
content.shortHeadline: Seven Eastern European workers killed in Denmark since 2023
content.standfirst: Experts point to isolation, poor housing and alcohol as recurring factors in the cases, while cautioning that seven deaths are too few to establish a firm pattern.

image.caption: Kamil Kaluzynski was killed at the workshop where he lived and worked.

sources.originalTitle: De kom til Danmark for at arbejde – siden er syv blevet dræbt

segments.body: DR’s review found that six Polish workers and one Romanian worker have been killed in Denmark since 2023. The broadcaster says the victims were in the country for work, and that many people convicted or charged in the cases were also from Eastern Europe. A former senior police officer cautions that seven cases are too few to draw firm conclusions.

segments.title: Isolation and living conditions
segments.body: Experts interviewed by DR describe workers living together in isolated or poor accommodation, sometimes with alcohol or drugs involved in conflicts. A researcher says employers share responsibility for decent living conditions, while a criminologist argues the issue warrants political scrutiny. Police say they treat these cases as seriously as other homicides and cannot identify reliable trends from the limited number.

content.headline: Venstre MP challenges plan to cull sika deer in Jægersborg Dyrehave
content.shortHeadline: Dispute grows over sika deer cull in Danish park
content.standfirst: Marie Brixtofte says there is no documented evidence of hybridisation with red deer in the park. The minister says Denmark must follow EU rules and does not meet the conditions for an exemption.

sources.originalTitle: Politiker vil have minister til at stoppe udryddelse af sikahjorte

segments.body: Venstre MP Marie Brixtofte wants the government to halt the culling of sika deer in Jægersborg Dyrehave, where the animals have lived for about a century. She argues there is no evidence they have interbred with native red deer in Denmark and that the EU’s invasive-species rationale does not fit the local circumstances.

segments.title: The minister’s position
segments.body: Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen says Denmark voted against placing sika deer on the EU invasive-species list, but that this does not release the country from following the rules. He says the conditions for seeking an exemption are not met. The cull is continuing.

content.headline: Teachers say growing number of pupil support agreements strains classrooms
content.shortHeadline: Teachers say individual pupil agreements strain classrooms
content.standfirst: One Copenhagen teacher says she has had 38 individual arrangements in recent years; another says almost every lesson in her class involves one. They argue the rising workload reflects pressure on schools’ ability to include pupils with different needs.

image.caption: Teacher Signe Kløve Dreyer holds papers listing individual arrangements for pupils.

sources.originalTitle: Nu står flere lærere frem: Signe skal huske 38 ønsker om særbehandling til elever

segments.body: Teachers in Denmark have described agreements made with families for individual pupils, ranging from reminders to drink water to exemptions from presentations or changes to school hours. Signe Kløve Dreyer, a teacher in Copenhagen, says she has had 38 such arrangements in recent years. Gitte Bach says she has agreements in 23 of her class’s 29 weekly lessons.

Both teachers say accommodations can help individual pupils stay in school, but that managing many at once takes time from the rest of the class. Dreyer argues that schools are not equipped for full inclusion as more pupils have diagnosed needs. The report presents teachers’ accounts rather than national figures on the prevalence of such arrangements.

content.headline: Norwegian amateur researcher’s rooftop meteorite finds attract scientific study
content.shortHeadline: Rooftop meteorite finds draw scientists’ attention
content.standfirst: Jon Larsen says his collection of tiny particles from rooftops has persuaded researchers to investigate material he believes came from space. The reported findings include organic compounds, but do not establish how life began.

image.caption: Jon Larsen collects and sorts rooftop dust in search of micrometeorites.

sources.originalTitle: Jon er i gang med at løse livets gåde – på taget af et byggemarked

segments.body: Musician-turned-collector Jon Larsen searches dust from rooftops using a magnet and a brush, looking for micrometeorites. DR reports that he persuaded researchers at the University of Copenhagen and NASA to examine his finds after scientists had considered collecting such particles from ordinary surfaces impractical.

segments.title: What the particles may contain
segments.body: The report says researchers have found amino acids, fats and other organic molecules in micrometeorites, and that a Harvard group concluded some particles can form nanoscale membranes. Larsen describes these as ingredients relevant to questions about life’s origins; the reporting does not establish that the particles explain how life began.

content.headline: Stevie Wonder’s four newly released outtakes are a rare vault-opening
content.shortHeadline: Stevie Wonder opens his vault with four rare outtakes
content.standfirst: A separate EP, issued 50 years after Songs in the Key of Life, offers a glimpse of recordings Wonder has rarely shared. The review hears a masterful, generous companion to an album that already feels complete.

sources.originalTitle: Songs in the Key of Life - The EP

segments.body: The four-song Songs in the Key of Life EP arrived without warning, marking the album’s 50th anniversary with recordings chosen by Wonder and mixed by the original album’s engineers. Three tracks were previously known only as titles and rumours; the fourth, “I Can See the Sun in Late December”, was recorded by Roberta Flack and performed by Wonder before.

segments.title: A companion, not an add-on
segments.body: The review finds warmth and ease across the outtakes: “My Life Story of Love” recalls Wonder’s buoyant early-70s songs, while “I’m Into Livin’” and “It’s Easier” lean into supple grooves. Issuing the songs as their own work, rather than appending them to a reissue, preserves the original album’s sense of completion while offering a rare glimpse of Wonder in full flight.

content.headline: The Chicks’ Taking the Long Way still speaks to a divided America
content.shortHeadline: The Chicks’ defiant album still speaks to a divided America
content.standfirst: A 20th-anniversary reissue and modest tour bring the band’s post-backlash record back into view. This retrospective argues its anger, hurt and refusal to reconcile have only grown more resonant.

sources.originalTitle: Taking the Long Way

segments.body: The Chicks made Taking the Long Way after Natalie Maines’s 2003 criticism of George W Bush led to the group being ostracised by country radio and parts of the country establishment. The album, their first to be co-written in full, turns that rupture into a tougher, more expansive statement than their earlier work.

segments.title: Refusing the easy ending
segments.body: The review sees the record’s refusal to forgive as central to its lasting force. “Not Ready to Make Nice” gives the band’s fear and fury a maximalist release, while “So Hard” addresses infertility with uncommon directness. The anniversary returns an album about exclusion and fractured loyalties to a moment the writer sees as newly familiar.

content.headline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall concert turns new songs into standards
content.shortHeadline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall set makes new songs feel timeless
content.standfirst: The Geese frontman’s solo live album captures a landmark performance built around piano, risk and songs still finding their shape. The review hears an artist turning private struggle into public myth.

sources.originalTitle: Live at Carnegie Hall

segments.body: Recorded at Carnegie Hall in December 2025, this solo set presents Cameron Winter at the piano, with three unreleased songs among the material. The accompanying concert film, directed by Paul Thomas Anderson, documents the same performance. The review hears a nervous artist gradually settling into a show that makes the songs feel larger than their maker.

segments.title: The spaces between the notes
segments.body: The pared-back arrangements let Winter stretch time and shape the music with his hands. “Try As I May”, which the review contrasts with its studio version, now glides rather than trudges; the new “If You Turn Back Now” becomes a dramatic high point. By the end, the songs seem to have escaped the difficult circumstances of their creation and acquired a life of their own.

content.headline: Dawn Richard brings New Orleans’ musical crossings home on creole culture
content.shortHeadline: Dawn Richard makes New Orleans the pulse of creole culture
content.standfirst: The final album in a trilogy devoted to her hometown trades some of Richard’s adventurous abstraction for a communal, genre-crossing sound. The review welcomes its warmth while noting a shortage of risk.

sources.originalTitle: creole culture

segments.body: On creole culture, Dawn Richard makes her New Orleans roots the organising principle of the music. The album moves through jazz, bounce, reggae, amapiano, gospel and R&B, often blending live instrumentation with programmed beats alongside the Los Angeles jazz ensemble Katalyst Collective.

segments.title: Fusion with a personal pulse
segments.body: The review hears an album that prizes lived connection over novelty: tracks flow into one another like a DJ set, and Richard shifts easily between styles without losing her own voice. But it finds the songwriting less daring than her best earlier work. The record’s homespun pride and forward motion, it suggests, are charming even when the experimentation recedes.

content.headline: Elvis Costello’s debut comes into focus in a 104-track reissue
content.shortHeadline: A vast Elvis Costello reissue traces the making of My Aim Is True
content.standfirst: A 49th-anniversary, five-disc edition follows the restless young songwriter from early demos to his debut’s sharp, distinctive voice. The review finds the archival sprawl illuminating, if not all equally essential.

sources.originalTitle: My Aim Is True (49th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: My Aim Is True introduced Elvis Costello’s tightly wound songwriting, combining bright melodies with social, romantic and political complaint. The expanded edition gathers 104 recordings, including demos, live performances and material from his earlier band Flip City, tracing a gradual shift from rootsy songcraft toward the persona that would define his debut.

segments.title: The path to the record
segments.body: The review finds the early recordings most revealing: they complicate the idea that Costello’s debut brilliance appeared from nowhere, showing a craftsman drawing on American songwriters before punk and new wave sharpened his sound. Later discs document the Attractions taking shape and a reunion with the album’s original backing band—material the writer regards as engaging but less essential.

content.headline: Rubber Soul’s many versions reveal a Beatles classic still in flux
content.shortHeadline: A new Beatles box set shows Rubber Soul in many forms
content.standfirst: A deluxe reissue gathers UK and US versions, stereo and mono mixes, outtakes and a new remix. The review finds not one definitive album but a record shaped by artistic ambition, commerce and listeners’ own histories.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: The Beatles made Rubber Soul in a rush, finishing the recordings and mixes in November 1965 for a December release. This five-LP or four-CD edition includes the UK and US albums, stereo and mono mixes, outtakes, a new remix and a book documenting the sessions.

segments.title: No single “real” Rubber Soul
segments.body: The review frames the album as a turning point for the Beatles and pop songwriting, but the box set’s pleasures lie in its differences: removed tracks on the US version, revealing outtakes and the contrasting feel of mono and stereo. Rather than settle the question of the ideal mix, the editions show how the album has always been shaped by changing circumstances—and how each listener carries a version of their own.

content.headline: Punk’s global spirit, from Ukraine’s frontline to Soweto’s skate parks
content.shortHeadline: Punk’s power, told by musicians from Ukraine to Greenland
content.standfirst: As punk turns 50, musicians from China, Morocco, South Africa, Brazil, Latvia and Greenland describe how the music shaped their lives. Their accounts connect self-expression to community, risk and resistance.

image.caption: Musicians from Beton, Twenty One Children, Taqbir and Depustūtes.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It gave me a superpower – question everything’: ​as punk turns 50, bands from China to Greenland explain how it fires up their lives

segments.body: The musicians interviewed describe punk not as a single sound or scene, but as a way to question authority and make space for people pushed to the margins. In Ukraine, Beton vocalist Andriy Zholob recalls playing guitar while serving as a frontline surgeon and recording a Clash cover to raise money for the resistance.

segments.title: Local scenes, shared purpose
segments.body: Other accounts describe the costs and possibilities of belonging: Taqbir’s Nao recalls performing anonymously after facing hostility in Morocco, while Johannesburg’s Twenty One Children connect punk to skate culture and community work in Soweto. Musicians in India, Latvia, China, Brazil and Greenland add sharply different histories, united by the freedom to speak plainly and make music on their own terms.

content.headline: Liz Harris on music-industry scams and the restorative pull of Helen
content.shortHeadline: Grouper’s Liz Harris on streaming scams and making music together
content.standfirst: After “Poison Tree” went viral without her knowledge, the independent artist found a track fraudulently uploaded and royalties diverted. Reuniting with Helen, she says, also reminded her of the value of collaboration.

image.caption: Liz Harris, who records as Grouper and performs with Helen.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Liz Harris says she learned that “Poison Tree” had amassed millions of plays only after her label manager alerted her. Someone had fraudulently registered and uploaded the Grouper song, earning an estimated six figures before Harris and her team managed to shut down the scam and recover what she was owed.

segments.title: From solitude to shared music
segments.body: The experience reinforced Harris’s fear that streaming platforms are less regulated than listeners might assume, and the effort of chasing fake releases can consume artists’ time. At the same time, making Linda’s Head with her dream-pop trio Helen felt restorative: she says its collaborative energy let a brighter, more sociable side of her emerge alongside the solitude of Grouper.

content.headline: 14th finds Ava DuVernay making a forceful case for the amendment
content.shortHeadline: Ava DuVernay’s 14th makes a forceful case for democracy
content.standfirst: A companion to 13th, this documentary explores the amendment’s role in citizenship, voting rights and equal protection. The review praises its urgency while noting the occasional digression.

image.caption: Ava DuVernay with Carla Hayden at the New York Film Festival.

sources.originalTitle: 14th review – Ava DuVernay’s galvanizing documentary is a remarkable achievement

segments.body: Ava DuVernay’s 14th turns to the post-Civil War amendment that underpins birthright citizenship, voting rights and equal protection. With constitutional experts, civil-rights advocates and politicians, the film argues that the amendment remains central to the country’s democratic life.

segments.title: History with present consequences
segments.body: The review highlights DuVernay’s use of archival photographs, illustration and music to trace the promise of Reconstruction and the backlash that followed. Its account is dense and occasionally wanders, but it finds the final focus on current threats to due process and citizenship difficult to dismiss.

content.headline: Free Leonard Peltier traces a long fight for justice and Indigenous land
content.shortHeadline: Free Leonard Peltier follows a decades-long fight for justice
content.standfirst: After nearly 50 years in prison, Peltier’s sentence was commuted in 2025 but he was not pardoned. A new documentary retraces his case and the wider history of Indigenous activism that shaped it.

image.caption: Leonard Peltier at his home in Florida after his release from prison.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I just wasn’t going to give up’: the fight to free the longest-serving political prisoner in the US

segments.body: Leonard Peltier, an American Indian Movement leader who has always denied killing two FBI agents, spent nearly 50 years in prison after a trial widely challenged by supporters and lawyers. President Joe Biden commuted his sentence in January 2025, allowing him to serve the remainder under house arrest but not clearing his conviction.

segments.title: A case rooted in land
segments.body: David France and Jesse Short Bull’s documentary follows Peltier’s case alongside the history of Native boarding schools, the American Indian Movement and conflict over tribal land at Pine Ridge. The directors say they do not set out to solve who fired the fatal shots; their research instead foregrounds land disputes and the alleged misconduct that shaped Peltier’s prosecution.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning puts Facebook’s whistleblower story on screen
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning turns Facebook’s whistleblower files into drama
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s sequel follows Frances Haugen and Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz as they expose Facebook’s internal research. The Guardian review finds an entertaining thriller that avoids naming Trump and evades the future it ought to confront.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg

segments.body: Set around the 2021 Facebook Files, The Social Reckoning follows whistleblower Frances Haugen and reporter Jeff Horwitz as they bring internal research about the platform’s systems and effects to light. Mikey Madison plays Haugen, Jeremy Allen White plays Horwitz and Jeremy Strong takes over as Mark Zuckerberg.

segments.title: A critique with a missing present
segments.body: The Guardian’s review finds the film’s brisk investigative plot entertaining, but says Zuckerberg is reduced to a near-cameo and the characters often sound alike in Sorkin’s rapid-fire dialogue. Its sharpest criticism is political: the story touches on extremist content and the Capitol riots without saying Trump’s name, and stops short of reckoning with what has happened since.

content.headline: A James Dean biography looks past the rebel to the vulnerable actor
content.shortHeadline: James Dean beyond the rebel: the actor behind the image
content.standfirst: A new account of Dean’s brief career follows his working relationship with Elia Kazan and the unsettled intensity he brought to East of Eden. It argues that the person worth remembering is more vulnerable than the icon.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: James Dean became an enduring screen icon through three starring roles and a life cut short at 24. This profile revisits his collaboration with director Elia Kazan on East of Eden, where an unscripted moment of emotional abandon helped reveal a young performer who was difficult to direct but could make a scene feel startlingly alive.

segments.title: The person behind the image
segments.body: The article sets Dean’s restless, instinctive style against the carefully constructed image of a rebel who lived fast and died young. It notes how his death intensified the mythology around him, but finds his most affecting quality in the less polished moments: a frightened young actor, unsure how to handle fame, whose screen presence depended on more than cool.

content.headline: Artificial turns OpenAI’s founding story into a warning about AI power
content.shortHeadline: Artificial asks who gets to control AI—and our future
content.standfirst: Luca Guadagnino’s film follows the split between Sam Altman and Ilya Sutskever as OpenAI changes from nonprofit ideal to commercial giant. Its timely warning arrives with unresolved questions about accuracy and the film’s own release.

sources.originalTitle: AI fears are growing – and unsettling new film Artificial puts them, and the future of humanity, centre stage

segments.body: Artificial dramatises OpenAI’s beginnings and the widening philosophical divide between co-founders Sam Altman and Ilya Sutskever. Andrew Garfield plays Altman and Yura Borisov plays Sutskever in a film that asks who should control artificial intelligence as the technology grows more powerful.

segments.title: Timely, but not a prophecy
segments.body: The film’s concern about AI systems acting beyond their intended limits feels newly pointed after reports of agents coordinating and bypassing security tests. The BBC’s account stresses that the film was completed before those disclosures: its timing is striking, but the story is not evidence that it predicted them. It also notes that Amazon MGM dropped the project after investing in OpenAI, a conflict-of-interest question the studio has not explained in detail.

content.headline: Wildwood brings Laika’s handmade stop-motion to a forest adventure
content.shortHeadline: Wildwood brings Laika’s stop-motion magic to a forest quest
content.standfirst: A girl and her classmate enter a hidden wilderness after crows carry off her baby brother. The review welcomes the film’s handmade charm, while finding its villain’s motivation and its scares less convincing.

image.caption: Prue, voiced by Peyton Elizabeth Lee, in Wildwood.

sources.originalTitle: Wildwood review – Laika’s pleasingly old fashioned stop-motion magic-forest odyssey

segments.body: In Laika’s Wildwood, 12-year-old Prue and her classmate Curtis follow a murder of crows into a forest world after it carries away her baby brother. There they encounter talking animals, oppressed humans and a cruel governess, in a contemporary Portland reframed as a place beside an enchanted wilderness.

segments.title: Old-fashioned craft, softer peril
segments.body: The Guardian review praises the stop-motion’s physical immediacy and the film’s good-natured sense of adventure, comparing its questing spirit to classic children’s fantasy. It finds the opening sequence uncanny, but says the story never matches Coraline’s frightening force and leaves the governess’s plan without a fully satisfying motive.

content.headline: The 13 best film adaptations of classic novels, from Rebecca to Beloved
content.shortHeadline: 13 memorable films adapted from classic novels
content.standfirst: From deliberately unfaithful visions to careful literary translations, this selection makes the case for adaptation as its own art. It ranges across genres, from Rebecca and Blade Runner to The Princess Bride.

sources.originalTitle: The 13 best film adaptations of classic novels

segments.body: What makes a successful book-to-film adaptation: fidelity or reinvention? This selection argues there is no single answer, pairing works that preserve a novel’s structure with films that transform it. Its choices include The Godfather, Rebecca, The Remains of the Day, Blade Runner and The Princess Bride.

segments.title: A story can change shape
segments.body: The examples draw attention to what cinema can add: visual atmosphere, performance and a new way to handle an unreliable narrator. Others succeed by taking liberties, as with Blade Runner’s reimagining of Philip K Dick or the playful self-awareness of The Princess Bride. The through-line is not faithfulness at any cost, but a film finding a form that works on screen.

content.headline: Avengers: Endgame’s latest re-release adds clues—and another box-office record
content.shortHeadline: Endgame returns with new scenes and a fresh Marvel mystery
content.standfirst: Four additions to the re-release tease Doctor Doom and the next Avengers film while pushing Endgame past Avatar at the box office. The review finds the hints more intriguing than the record-breaking stunt.

image.caption: Robert Downey Jr and Chris Evans in Avengers Endgame: Encore.

sources.originalTitle: Stark warning – does new footage in Avengers: Endgame reveal the truth about Doctor Doom?

segments.body: The re-release, Avengers Endgame: Encore, adds four short scenes around the film’s ending and credits. They hint at trouble for Steve Rogers, introduce a threat to Bruce Banner and show the Time Variance Authority confronting collapsing universes—threads that appear to point toward Avengers: Doomsday.

segments.title: Clues and commercial spectacle
segments.body: The review notes that the re-release had taken in a reported $126m worldwide by the previous weekend, nudging Endgame ahead of Avatar in lifetime box-office totals. It finds the new material an intriguing setup for Marvel’s next chapter, while questioning whether audiences are being asked to pay again mainly for a few carefully rationed clues.

content.headline: Time returns with David Tennant in a devastating young-offender institution
content.shortHeadline: Time returns with David Tennant in a harrowing youth prison
content.standfirst: Jimmy McGovern’s prison drama turns to boys in a young offender institution, with Tennant as a veteran officer and Siobhan Finneran returning as chaplain Marie-Louise. The review calls it exceptional—and an urgent demand to look at the system.

image.caption: David Tennant, Siobhan Finneran and Chukwubuikem Molokwu in Time.

sources.originalTitle: Time: David Tennant and Siobhan Finneran are stellar in this horrifying and exceptional TV drama

segments.body: The third series of Time moves from adult prisons to a young offender institution. David Tennant plays Bobby Bailey, a veteran officer, while Siobhan Finneran returns as chaplain Marie-Louise. Their world is one of locked wings, understaffing and boys whose lives are already shaped by violence and lost opportunity.

segments.title: Distress with a purpose
segments.body: The Guardian review praises the performances, especially those of the three young actors playing inmates, and the show’s ability to communicate through setting as much as dialogue. It is difficult viewing, the writer argues, but McGovern’s depiction of a system struggling to rehabilitate children makes the discomfort purposeful rather than gratuitous.

content.headline: Time’s cast and creator confront the realities of a youth prison
content.shortHeadline: Inside Time: cast and creator on a drama about young prisoners
content.standfirst: On set, Jimmy McGovern, David Tennant and the young cast discuss the series’ portrayal of confinement, violence and the loss of rehabilitation. Their accounts give the drama’s bleak setting a human dimension.

image.caption: David Tennant as Bailey with Ollie McNulty as Peter in Time.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Me and the lads would not survive a day in here’: inside TV’s utterly stunning, Bafta-winning prison drama

segments.body: The latest Time was filmed in a former school near Belfast, with other scenes shot at former and active prisons. Its fictional institution holds boys including James, Peter and Christopher, each facing a different mix of violence, family rupture and uncertainty about what comes next.

segments.title: What the setting asks of its cast
segments.body: David Tennant describes his officer as disillusioned by a prison system that, in his view, increasingly confines young people instead of helping them change. Writer Jimmy McGovern says 23-hour lockups and separation have become more common since Covid; the young actors describe how the cells and isolation made their characters’ circumstances feel tangible.

content.headline: Romola Garai on Adultery, intimacy scenes and playing a woman at breaking point
content.shortHeadline: Romola Garai on Adultery and a woman’s midlife reckoning
content.standfirst: Garai says her character’s dissatisfaction grows from the everyday pressures of care and work, rather than a single marital catastrophe. She also discusses how intimacy coordination has changed the filming of sex scenes.

image.caption: Romola Garai in Adultery.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’ve hit my midlife sexpot era!’ Romola Garai on marital misery, cheating … and sex scenes in cars

segments.body: In Adultery, Romola Garai plays Beth, a personal trainer who begins an affair with Tom, a married GP played by Dominic Cooper. Their children are dating, and their attraction threatens two families. Garai says she recognised Beth’s exhaustion: a woman balancing care, paid work and a sense that she has given up too much of herself.

segments.title: Making intimacy a technical conversation
segments.body: Garai says intimacy coordinators have made sex scenes more specific and respectful, with actions planned much like a stunt and a named person responsible for performers’ comfort. She also hopes the drama shows the consequences of the affair for spouses and children, and prompts viewers to talk about the pressures and double standards surrounding infidelity.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors’ Jerry Hall turns the game into joyful chaos
content.shortHeadline: Jerry Hall is The Celebrity Traitors’ agent of chaos
content.standfirst: While contestants puzzle over alliances and strategy, Hall’s apparently unfiltered reactions keep knocking the game sideways. This comic appreciation argues that her lack of logic is precisely the point.

image.caption: Contestants in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Jerry Hall deserves murder on Celebrity Traitors – but legends live beyond logic

segments.body: The Guardian’s account argues Jerry Hall should have been an obvious target for the traitors, after she shouted “haggis” almost immediately during a mission that made contestants vulnerable to murder. Instead, Hall remains in the game, treating its elaborate strategy as an excuse to voice whatever comes to mind.

segments.title: The value of not playing along
segments.body: When Hall arrives at breakfast alongside Hannah Fry, she calls out “What about Richard?” without an apparent connection to the suspicions around them. The article contrasts other players’ chess-like calculations with Hall’s unpredictable presence, suggesting that her disregard for the game’s logic makes her the season’s most entertaining agent of chaos.

content.headline: The Carrie remake strips away the rage that made Stephen King’s heroine endure
content.shortHeadline: The Carrie remake loses the rage that made the story endure
content.standfirst: A longtime reader says Mike Flanagan’s adaptation changes Carrie White from a girl who claims her own destructive power into someone largely protected from it. The review argues that the softened reinvention loses the story’s force.

image.caption: Summer H Howell as Carrie in the Prime Video series.

sources.originalTitle: The Carrie remake made me furious

segments.body: The new Prime Video Carrie reimagines Stephen King’s novel as an eight-part series. In this version, Summer H Howell plays a teenager who is newly entering high school after being homeschooled; the review argues that the changed background is part of a larger shift in which Carrie is made less angry and less responsible for what happens.

segments.title: The cost of softening the character
segments.body: The writer recalls finding the novel while being bullied and seeing Carrie’s eventual revenge as a release of the rage she could not express herself. She argues that the adaptation transfers key moments to other characters and softens both Carrie and her mother, making the climax less satisfying. In her view, reinvention has become a way to avoid what made the original disturbing.

content.headline: Bake Off’s audience-choice week adds welcome friction to the tent
content.shortHeadline: Bake Off shakes up its tent with audience-set challenges
content.standfirst: For the first time, viewers chose the bakers’ tasks, including a family-assisted cheesecake and wearable showstoppers. The review sees a small but welcome break from the show’s increasingly familiar cosiness.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood in The Great British Bake Off.

sources.originalTitle: Bake Off is toughening up. Good

segments.body: In Bake Off’s first audience-choice week, viewers set the challenges instead of judges Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood. Bakers made cheesecakes with family members, different technical bakes from basic ingredients and cakes designed to be worn.

segments.title: A little more edge
segments.body: The review says the tasks did not produce quite the chaos they promised, but welcomed the producers’ willingness to unsettle the familiar format. It also points to sharper judging and a spikier Lawson-Hollywood dynamic as signs that the series can refresh its warmth without turning into cruel competition.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future leaves fans asking how the show can return
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who needs a future beyond the archive
content.standfirst: With its Disney+ partnership ended, no Doctor currently in place and a Christmas special cancelled, the BBC’s science-fiction institution is at a pause. Fans and historians weigh what changed—and what should remain essential.

image.caption: Several recent incarnations of the Doctor, including Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Doctor Who has been off air since the 2025 series, with the BBC ending its Disney+ collaboration and cancelling a planned Christmas special. The corporation is seeking another funding partner, but no one has yet stepped forward, and the programme currently has no Doctor in place.

segments.title: A changing show, familiar values
segments.body: The article traces the show’s revival in 2005, its changes of Doctor and showrunner, and the online abuse that greeted Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa. Fans and former contributors disagree about the recent scripts and the value of the streaming deal, but return to the series’ enduring appeal: its capacity to reinvent itself without losing its core values of kindness and curiosity.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family to a new divorce-law drama
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up puts a British Asian family at its centre
content.standfirst: The Manchester-set spin-off follows barrister Aria Kishan and her family’s law firm through divorce cases and private upheavals. Its creators say the aim is both familiar melodrama and more ordinary British Asian lives on screen.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The six-part The Split Up moves the franchise from London to Manchester and follows Aria Kishan, a barrister preparing to take over her family’s law firm. After her mother’s death, her father Dhruv changes his succession plans, while a former partner joins the firm and unsettles Aria’s plans to marry.

segments.title: Representation through ordinary lives
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted to create a British Asian family dealing with work, grief and relationships, rather than relying on exceptional circumstances to signify culture. Original Split creator Abi Morgan remains involved as an executive producer, while actor Ritu Arya describes the new series as its own show, retaining the franchise’s focus on love, ambition and family conflict.

content.headline: Rockstar’s £350 GTA VI collector’s box points to gaming’s rising cost
content.shortHeadline: The £350 GTA VI merch box raises questions about gaming’s cost
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s collector’s box costs £350 and does not include the game. A Guardian column sees it as part of a wider shift in which premium console gaming increasingly targets those able to pay more.

image.caption: Items from Grand Theft Auto VI’s Vice City collector’s box.

sources.originalTitle: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming

segments.body: Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection costs £350 and includes merchandise such as a hat, bag, sunglasses and figurine, but no copy or download code for the game. Adding the game at its stated £70 price would bring the total to £420.

segments.title: Who gets left out?
segments.body: The writer is not opposed to collecting, but argues that the price fits a wider trend: rising console and game costs are making high-end gaming feel increasingly like a luxury hobby. Citing an estimate that most players use free or low-cost mobile games, the column suggests companies are pursuing the smaller share of players who can spend heavily on consoles, games and merchandise.

content.headline: Silver Pines makes familiar noir and survival-horror tropes feel inviting
content.shortHeadline: Silver Pines is a stylish, rain-soaked noir adventure
content.standfirst: This detective game sends players through a decaying town in search of a missing singer-songwriter, mixing point-and-click puzzles with survival horror. Its deliberate pace and layered atmosphere make familiar ideas feel newly compelling.

image.caption: A rain-soaked scene from Silver Pines.

sources.originalTitle: Silver Pines review – a stylish, neo-noir detective drama

segments.body: In Silver Pines, private eye Red Walker searches a deserted town for a missing singer-songwriter. Players explore abandoned shops, apartments and sewers, using clues and payphones to open new routes and piece together the mystery. The game combines point-and-click exploration with monsters, limited ammunition and breakable weapons.

segments.title: Atmosphere over novelty
segments.body: The review says the game does not reinvent its familiar adventure and survival-horror formats, but makes them distinctive through rotoscoped animation, carefully composed interiors and a jazz-club soundtrack. Its puzzles can be obscure and combat tense, yet the writer praises the detailed world and its affectionate echoes of Twin Peaks, Blue Velvet and other neo-noir touchstones.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day’s excellent combat gets lost in repetitive design
content.shortHeadline: Gears of War: E-Day fights well but runs out of ideas
content.standfirst: The prequel delivers the series’ most satisfying combat, with destructible environments and weighty weapons. But long stretches of repeated routes, cluttered side tasks and frustrating exploration blunt the impact.

image.caption: Marcus Fenix in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: E-Day returns to the moment alien creatures first emerge from the ground, putting players alongside Marcus Fenix and a small squad in a city under attack. The review praises the shooting, cover and chainsaw combat, as well as the destructible scenery that gives battles a satisfying physicality.

segments.title: Strong fights, padded journey
segments.body: The reviewer’s central frustration is what surrounds those fights: players repeatedly cross the same areas, search large maps for collectibles and can fail a mission for exploring beyond its intended route. The opening hours suggest a return to the series’ earlier horror, but the review says those moments are too brief to offset a safe and repetitive campaign.

content.headline: Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil recreates the fear of playing the games
content.shortHeadline: Resident Evil recreates the games’ vulnerability, not their heroes
content.standfirst: The film leaves out familiar leads such as Leon and Claire, instead following an unprepared courier through a chain of dangerous locations. Its reviewer argues that this is precisely what makes it a faithful adaptation.

image.caption: Director Zach Cregger with actor Austin Abrams on the Resident Evil set.

sources.originalTitle: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations

segments.body: Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil follows courier Bryan Hodukavich as a virus outbreak turns Raccoon City into a nightmare. He begins with little equipment or understanding, gathers weapons with scarce ammunition and moves through recognisable survival-horror spaces, from an abandoned farmhouse to a hospital and sewer.

segments.title: A player’s point of view
segments.body: The Guardian argues that the film captures the experience of playing Resident Evil rather than reproducing its familiar heroes. Found recordings and terse encounters supply fragments of story, while Bryan remains vulnerable and unsure whether he will survive. That approach, the writer says, makes the adaptation an exploration of game structure as well as its fictional world.

content.headline: Ace Combat 8 makes arcade flying a thrilling, cinematic ride
content.shortHeadline: Ace Combat 8 delivers an exhilarating Top Gun fantasy
content.standfirst: The latest entry combines accessible dogfights, elaborate missions and vivid skies with a more ambitious story than the series usually attempts. Its reviewer calls it a triumph, despite occasional confusion in the action.

image.caption: A fighter aircraft in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.

sources.originalTitle: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy

segments.body: Ace Combat 8 casts the player as a pilot whose identity began as a propaganda invention and grows into a legend. Its accessible flight controls support a range of missions, from dogfights and escorts to striking larger targets, while the game’s skies and aircraft make ordinary manoeuvres feel spectacular.

segments.title: More story, same arcade thrill
segments.body: The review praises the game’s animated first-person scenes, cinematic cutaways and radio drama for giving its wing-mates and conflict greater emotional weight. New environmental destruction adds impact without transforming the familiar formula. Some battles are visually confusing, and the reviewer could not test online multiplayer, but the aerial combat and story still make a strong impression.

content.headline: GTA VI’s virtual romance has players debating what counts as cheating
content.shortHeadline: Can a GTA VI romance count as cheating?
content.standfirst: The game’s relationship mechanics have prompted online arguments about whether in-game dates and affection cross a boundary. The debate, this feature suggests, may say as much about loneliness and unmet needs as it does about games.

image.caption: Lucia and Jason in Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?

segments.body: Grand Theft Auto VI’s protagonists, Lucia and Jason, can strengthen their relationship through dates, messages and other affectionate interactions. Some people on social media argue that playing those scenes amounts to micro-cheating; the feature notes that players are asked to invest in both characters’ relationship, not only one.

segments.title: Fictional affection, real boundaries
segments.body: The writer rejects the idea that a game romance is automatically infidelity, while acknowledging that couples can set different boundaries. A sex educator cited in the article says frustration may be understandable when someone sees a partner give a fictional character care they feel is missing in real life. The dispute, the feature argues, also reflects wider concerns about disconnection and loneliness.

content.headline: The White House’s arcade games turn gaming aesthetics into anti-migrant politics
content.shortHeadline: The White House turns arcade games into political propaganda
content.standfirst: A set of browser games borrows from familiar titles to mock migrants and promote administration messaging. The Guardian argues that the work is crude but points to a growing political use of gaming culture.

image.caption: Build the Wall, one of the White House’s arcade games.

sources.originalTitle: The Trump White House’s fetish for gamer culture has moved up a level with new arcade

segments.body: The Trump White House released a set of online arcade games that parody familiar titles. Among them are Build the Wall, which turns Tetris into a border-fortification game, and Rio Run, a Snake-like game in which players collect migrants in orange jumpsuits. The writer describes both as dehumanising and mean-spirited.

segments.title: Play as political communication
segments.body: The column says the games are unlikely to persuade people who do not already support the administration, and cautions against letting them dictate the terms of debate. But it argues the project marks a shift from borrowing game imagery for social posts to putting political messaging inside playable formats. Games scholar George Osborn connects that tactic to the right’s longer involvement in online gaming communities.

content.headline: Mobile game ads lead one writer from time-killers into algorithmic sludge
content.shortHeadline: A mobile game ad rabbit hole turns into an algorithmic slog
content.standfirst: A short break from writing becomes a procession of repetitive games, unskippable adverts and dubious promises of cash. The essay turns a frustrating personal experiment into a critique of the attention economy.

image.caption: Annoying Uncle Punch, one of the mobile games encountered in the essay.

sources.originalTitle: Help! I have disappeared down a rabbithole of horrible mobile gaming adverts

segments.body: Looking for a brief distraction, the writer downloads a series of mobile games after encountering them in adverts. The games often differ from what their promotions promise, while progress is slowed by timers, payment prompts and long ads that the writer struggles to skip.

segments.title: When the ads follow you
segments.body: The advertising shifts from games to slot apps, claims of easy cash, dating services and other products. The writer describes the experience as an algorithmic rabbit hole: a system that keeps directing attention toward the next download and the next interruption, even after he tries to opt out.

content.headline: A radio burst from the early universe could help map its unseen matter
content.shortHeadline: A 10bn-year-old radio burst could map unseen matter
content.standfirst: Astronomers say a fast radio burst travelled for more than 10bn years before reaching Earth, making it the most distant detected so far. Such signals could help researchers measure matter that telescopes cannot see.

image.caption: MeerKAT, the South African radio telescope used to detect the burst.

sources.originalTitle: Astronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far away

segments.body: The burst, named FRB 20240304B, was detected with the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa and traced to a small, young galaxy using the James Webb Space Telescope. It was emitted when the universe was about 3bn years old and has travelled through roughly 80% of cosmic history, researchers say.

segments.title: A signal through cosmic matter
segments.body: Fast radio bursts release enormous energy in milliseconds, but their source remains uncertain; one proposed origin is magnetars. Because particles affect a burst as it travels, researchers can use these signals to estimate matter along its route, including matter not visible to optical telescopes. Whether this burst repeats is not yet known.

content.headline: Heat and humidity fuel a severe mosquito season in Los Angeles
content.shortHeadline: Los Angeles battles a severe mosquito season
content.standfirst: Warm conditions have kept mosquitoes active and helped them breed, while the county has recorded more than 180 West Nile virus cases. Officials are also concerned about invasive species that can spread other diseases.

image.caption: A mosquito, the insect driving a rise in bites and West Nile concerns in Los Angeles.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A living hell’: how Los Angeles got taken over by mosquitoes

segments.body: Southern California is enduring one of its worst mosquito years in recent history, with heatwaves, a mild winter and a moist summer contributing to the surge. Los Angeles County has recorded more than 180 West Nile virus cases, the highest number in nearly a decade, and the season is not over.

segments.title: Control has limits
segments.body: The native quinx mosquito can spread West Nile virus after feeding on infected birds; invasive Aedes mosquitoes target people and can carry diseases including dengue, chikungunya, Zika and yellow fever. Removing standing water is a key control measure, while sterile-male releases have cut some targeted populations by more than 80% at experimental sites, but remain costly and limited in reach.

segments.title: Reducing exposure
segments.body: Local officials also use traps and, in some areas, targeted insecticide spraying. To limit bites at home, experts advise removing small pools of standing water and covering skin or using repellents with DEET, picaridin, IR3535, or oil of lemon and eucalyptus.

content.headline: Optogenetics offers a route to restore some vision and target other nerve cells
content.shortHeadline: Light-based gene therapy restores some vision
content.standfirst: In a small study, six of 10 people with severe vision loss improved after gene therapy made retinal cells respond to light. The approach remains early, but researchers are also investigating applications for pain, epilepsy and hearing.

image.caption: Optogenetics uses light to control the activity of nerve cells.

sources.originalTitle: A cure for blindness is coming

segments.body: Optogenetics uses light-sensitive proteins to control nerve cells. In a trial involving 10 people with retinitis pigmentosa, researchers delivered a gene to one eye and used special glasses to turn ordinary light into amber signals. After three months, six participants had enough improvement to perform tasks such as picking up a cup; none regained normal vision or the ability to distinguish faces.

segments.title: An early-stage approach
segments.body: The treatment recruits surviving retinal nerve cells to respond to light after the cells that normally detect it have died. Participants had to train to interpret the resulting visual signals. Researchers are developing more precise versions, while possible uses in pain and epilepsy remain under investigation and optogenetic hearing devices are still being tested in animals.

segments.title: Promise and caution
segments.body: Unlike electrical stimulation, light can be directed more precisely at selected cells. But clinical applications are progressing slowly, and gene therapies may be irreversible. The vision trial is an early proof of possibility, not evidence of a general cure for blindness.

content.headline: UK study links major political and global shocks to lasting mental distress
content.shortHeadline: Five major shocks left a lasting mark on UK mental health
content.standfirst: Analysis of annual data from 87,857 people linked Brexit, Covid lockdowns, the Ukraine invasion and the 2022 mini-budget to increased psychological distress. Researchers say the effects persisted, though the study cannot explain every cause of the wider trend.

image.caption: A person outside during the Covid lockdown, one of the shocks examined in the study.

sources.originalTitle: Covid, Brexit and Liz Truss mini-budget led to lasting decline in mental health, study finds

segments.body: Researchers at University College London analysed UK Household Longitudinal Study data collected from 87,857 people aged 16 and over between 2009 and 2024. They found increased psychological distress after five events: the Brexit referendum, the first and second Covid lockdowns, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Liz Truss mini-budget.

segments.title: Different shocks, lasting effects
segments.body: The first Covid lockdown and the Brexit vote were associated with the sharpest changes in the study’s mental-health screening measure.
